meta.description: Not Publilius Syrus. The line is Benjamin Franklin's, printed in Poor Richard's Almanack for 1755 — though Syrus's sententiae do carry a plainer relative.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be at War with Your Vices, at Peace with Your Neighbours, and Let Every New Year Find You a Better Person'?
meta.ogDescription: It is Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack for 1755, not Publilius Syrus — though the Roman sententiae really do say "peace with men, war with vices."

answer.label: Not Publilius Syrus — Benjamin Franklin
answer.sourceLine: This sentence is Franklin’s: it was printed in Poor Richard improved — Poor Richard’s Almanack — for 1755, in the “Aspects” column beside December’s astronomical data, as “Be at War with your Vices, at Peace with your Neighbours, and let every New-Year find you a better Man.” Publilius Syrus’s collected sententiae do carry a barer Roman ancestor, Pacem cum hominibus habebis, bellum cum vitiis — peace with men, war with vices — but nothing about neighbours or the New Year, and Franklin, a famous borrower of proverbs, may himself have been polishing an older saying rather than coining one.

source.heading: Poor Richard’s Almanack, 1755

docMeta.dd: Poor Richard improved: Being an Almanack and Ephemeris of the Motions of the Sun and Moon … (Poor Richard’s Almanack) for 1755
The “Aspects” column, interleaved with the astronomical data for December
Sayings of Poor Richard, in Autobiography. Poor Richard. Letters (D. Appleton, 1904), p. 229

source.excerpt:
A long Life may not be good enough, but a good Life is long enough.

Be at War with your Vices, at Peace with your Neighbours, and let every New-Year find you a better Man.
trail: 1755 — The sentence appears in Franklin’s Poor Richard improved for 1755, in the “Aspects” column beside December’s astronomical data: “Be at War with your Vices, at Peace with your Neighbours, and let every New-Year find you a better Man.” Quote Investigator reproduces the page scan ↗.

1856 — Darius Lyman’s English Moral Sayings of Publius Syrus gives, as no. 636, the much plainer “Be at war with men’s vices, at peace with themselves” — no neighbours, no New Year. Read the 1856 translation ↗.

1883 — Victor Duruy’s History of Rome printed adages ascribed to Syrus, among them “Forgive others often, thyself never; for one must live at peace with men, but at war with one’s own vices” — under a footnote warning that “Interpolations have been made in this collection; some of these sentences do not belong to Syrus.” Quote Investigator quotes both the adage and the footnote ↗.
1904 — Franklin’s collected Autobiography. Poor Richard. Letters reprints the maxim word for word on page 229. Internet Archive full text ↗.
source.excerptNote: The almanac capitalised the salient words, spelled Neighbours with a u, hyphenated New-Year, and ended “a better Man”; the modern “better person” is a later update. This pairing with the “long Life” maxim is how the two lines sit on page 229 of Franklin’s collected Sayings of Poor Richard ↗.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: Benjamin Franklin
author.metaLine: 1706–1790 · American printer, scientist and Founding Father
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin printed Poor Richard’s Almanack from 1732 to 1758 under the pen name Richard Saunders, packing its margins with the proverbs that made him the most quoted American of his century. He was also a scientist, postmaster, diplomat and Founding Father — but by his own reckoning he wrote only about one proverb in ten himself, finding the rest in older anthologies and sharpening them. That habit is precisely why so many “Franklin” maxims, this one included, come with an argument attached.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Publilius Syrus is a magnet for this one, and not for nothing — the Roman collection really does contain a maxim about peace with men and war with vices. What it does not contain is this sentence.

items.why: The Latin sententiae attributed to Syrus include Pacem cum hominibus habebis, bellum cum vitiis — literally, you will have peace with men, war with vices — printed among the main Sententiae at The Latin Library ↗ — though the same text repeats that line word for word in its appendix of sayings falso inter Publilianas receptae, falsely received as Publilius’s, so even the Roman ancestor is not securely his. Darius Lyman’s standard 1856 English version renders a maxim as “Be at war with men’s vices, at peace with themselves” (no. 636 ↗). Neither mentions a neighbour or a new year, and Wikiquote’s Publilius Syrus page ↗ does not carry the popular sentence in any section.

items.tag: Printed it — may not have coined it
items.why: Franklin published the wording, but Quote Investigator ↗ says plainly that it does not know whether this advice originated with him, since many almanac sayings came from elsewhere. Wikipedia records that Franklin reckoned he wrote perhaps one proverb in ten ↗, finding the rest in anthologies.

In 1827, American newspapers ran a set headed “Ancient and Modern Maxims: Translated from the Spanish,” including “Have peace with all men, war with all vices, and concord with thyself” — with no credit to Franklin. Quote Investigator lists the printings ↗. It shows how widely the thought travelled, not that it is this sentence’s source.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence people share at New Year — vices, neighbours, a better man — is Benjamin Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1755. The Roman relative Publilius Syrus is credited with is the far barer “peace with men, war with vices.” Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why the Roman gets the credit
lead: Franklin’s almanacs were not essay collections. They were working calendars — sunrise tables, moon phases, planetary aspects — and the maxims were set in the gaps, a line at a time, where a reader’s eye would fall while checking the weather. This one sat in the December column of the almanac for 1755 — the last month in the book — which is why it reads as a New Year’s resolution.

The Syrus credit sticks because it is half true. The Roman collection does hold a sentence about keeping peace with men and war with vices, and the thought is old enough that it surfaces in an 1827 American newspaper as a Spanish maxim with nobody’s name on it. But the specific shape people quote — your vices, your neighbours, every New Year, a better man — is a printer’s compression, and it first appears under Franklin’s imprint.
context.detailsSummary: How a Roman maxim became a New Year’s resolution
detailsBody: The oldest layer is Latin: Pacem cum hominibus habebis, bellum cum vitiis, among the sententiae handed down under Publilius Syrus’s name. Even there the ground is soft — when Victor Duruy printed a set of Syrus adages in 1883, his own edition carried a footnote conceding that interpolations had been made and that some of the sentences do not belong to Syrus at all.

The middle layer is proverbial and unattributed: the 1827 “Ancient and Modern Maxims” column, translated from the Spanish, ran “Have peace with all men, war with all vices, and concord with thyself” without crediting anyone. The top layer is Franklin’s, and it is the one that survived — reprinted as a “Franklin Maxim” in the Cleveland Plain Dealer in 1894 and gathered into his collected writings in 1904.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator documents the sentence in the 1755 edition of Poor Richard's Almanack as "Be at War with your Vices, at Peace with your Neighbours, and let every New-Year find you a better Man," printed in the December "Aspects" column, and states that QI does not know if this advice originated with Franklin.

Quote Investigator reports that Victor Duruy's 1883 History of Rome (vol. 4, sect. 2, p. 327) printed adages ascribed to Publilius Syrus, including "Forgive others often, thyself never; for one must live at peace with men, but at war with one's own vices," with a footnote reading "Interpolations have been made in this collection; some of these sentences do not belong to Syrus."

Quote Investigator records that in 1827 the National Intelligencer and other papers printed "Ancient and Modern Maxims: Translated from the Spanish," including "Have peace with all men, war with all vices, and concord with thyself," not credited to Benjamin Franklin.

This Internet Archive item is Benjamin Franklin, "Autobiography. Poor Richard. Letters" (New York: D. Appleton and Company, 1904), with introduction and notes by Ainsworth R. Spofford, containing a "Sayings of Poor Richard" section.

The full text of the 1904 D. Appleton volume prints, on page 229 under "Sayings of Poor Richard," the lines "A long Life may not be good enough, but a good Life is long enough." and "Be at War with your Vices, at Peace with your Neighbours, and let every New-Year find you a better Man."

Darius Lyman's 1856 translation "The Moral Sayings of Publius Syrus, a Roman Slave" contains, as no. 636, "Be at war with men's vices, at peace with themselves," and contains no maxim about being at peace with your neighbours or about the New Year.

The Latin Library's text of Publilius Syrus prints "Pacem cum hominibus habebis, bellum cum vitiis." among the main Sententiae, and prints that same line again verbatim — along with a variant, "Cum hominibus pacem, bella cum vitiis habe." — under the heading "SENTENTIAE FALSO INTER PUBLILIANAS RECEPTAE."

Wikiquote's Publilius Syrus page does not contain the "at war with your vices, at peace with your neighbours, let every new year find you a better man" saying in any section, and describes Publilius Syrus as flourishing 85–43 BC, a Latin writer best known for his sententiae.

Wikipedia states Poor Richard's Almanack was published by Benjamin Franklin from 1732 to 1758 under the pseudonym "Richard Saunders," and that "Franklin didn't write most of Poor Richard's proverbs. By his own guess, he wrote perhaps one out of every ten; the rest he found in books, especially anthologies like Thomas Fuller's 1732 Gnomologia."

Google Books volume WPULAAAAYAAJ is Victor Duruy, "History of Rome and of the Roman People: From Its Origin to the Invasion of the Barbarians" — the volume Quote Investigator cites for the 1883 Publilius Syrus adages.
Wikipedia identifies Benjamin Franklin as an American Founding Father and polymath, 1706–1790.
Wikiquote's Benjamin Franklin page does not contain the "Be at war with your vices, at peace with your neighbours" saying in any section, including its Poor Richard's Almanack material.
